# Diagnosing the 1987 Mazda B2000 Turn Signal Flasher

When a vehicle's turn signals fail while the hazard lights function correctly, the issue is rarely a complete electrical failure of the switch or the bulbs themselves. This specific symptom profile points directly to the flasher unit. In automotive electrical systems, the flasher acts as a timing mechanism that interrupts the current flow to create the blinking effect. The fact that the hazards work indicates that power reaches the sockets and the ground paths are intact; the system is simply missing the pulsing signal required for directional indication.

On the 1987 Mazda B2000, the flasher unit is a standalone component rather than an integrated relay or fusable link. This design choice was common in vehicles of that era, allowing for modular replacement without rewiring the entire dashboard harness. The unit is typically located on the underside of the dashboard, accessible by removing the trim panel beneath the steering column. You will often find it mounted near the brake fluid reservoir or secured to a bracket adjacent to the turn signal stalk assembly.

Technically, the flasher operates as a thermal bimetallic switch. Inside the unit, two strips of metal with different coefficients of expansion are bonded together. As current flows through the filament connected to these strips, they heat up and bend, breaking the circuit. Once the circuit breaks, the strips cool down, snap back to their original shape, and close the circuit again. This mechanical action creates the on-off rhythm we see as blinking lights. Because this is a thermal device, it requires a specific amount of current to operate correctly. If the filament inside burns out or the bimetallic contacts weld together due to age or voltage spikes, the unit will fail.

The distinction between the turn signal flasher and the hazard relay is critical here. In many 1980s vehicles, including the B2000, there are two distinct physical units. The hazard switch simply bypasses the directional logic and sends full current to all four sockets simultaneously. Since both left and right indicators must light up for hazards to work, the internal filament of the flasher does not need to cycle as aggressively or at all in that specific mode; the circuit remains closed longer, keeping the lights steady. However, when you engage a standard turn signal, the system relies entirely on the flasher unit to interrupt the current every 0.6 to 1.2 seconds.

To verify the location and condition of the component, inspect the wiring harness leading to the under-dash area. Look for a small, cylindrical or rectangular plastic housing with two wires entering it. One wire connects to the power source via the ignition switch (or directly from the battery on some models), while the other connects to the turn signal stalk assembly. If this unit is removed and tested with a multimeter set to continuity mode, you should hear an audible click every time the meter probes touch the internal terminals if the thermal element is still responsive.

If the unit is indeed faulty, replacing it is a low-cost repair that restores function without modifying the vehicle's wiring diagram. Ensure you source a replacement rated for 12V DC and compatible with the specific bulb wattage of your B2000. Using a flasher designed for lower-wattage LED bulbs on an incandescent setup can sometimes cause rapid cycling or failure, though this is less relevant if the original bulbs are still in place. Always disconnect the battery before removing dashboard trim to prevent shorting the ECU or radio memory, even if the vehicle lacks a sophisticated computer system.
